Medications for Substance Use Disorders

naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram · buprenorphine, methadone · varenicline, nicotine replacementWhich maintenance drug, and when is it safe to start?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Drug script
Bottom line
  • Alcohol: naltrexone or acamprosate first line. Naltrexone can start while still drinking, but not with opioids or liver disease (acute hepatitis and liver failure included); acamprosate after abstinence, not with significant kidney impairment; disulfiram second line, after 48 hours abstinent
  • Opioids: buprenorphine or methadone maintenance first line for most patients; buprenorphine only once withdrawal signs show; naltrexone only after withdrawal is complete
  • Tobacco: varenicline most effective, then combination nicotine replacement, then bupropion
What it is

Relapse-prevention drugs, given alongside psychosocial treatment: for alcohol, considered in moderate to severe use disorder; for opioids, agonist maintenance for most patients

Mechanism

Naltrexone: mu-opioid antagonist less craving, fewer heavy drinking days; opioid euphoria blocked

Acamprosate: glutamate modulator less craving once abstinent; excreted mostly unchanged by the kidneys

Disulfiram: acetaldehyde dehydrogenase blocked acetaldehyde builds after a drink flushing, headache, tachycardia, nausea

Buprenorphine: partial mu agonist, high affinity, low efficacy a ceiling on respiratory depression

Methadone: long-acting full agonist long half-life, so it accumulates

Varenicline: nicotinic partial agonist less withdrawal and craving; a lapse rewards less

Used for

Alcohol: naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram

Opioids: buprenorphine (often with naloxone), methadone, long-acting naltrexone

Tobacco: nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion, all first line, ranked by efficacy in step 7

Risks

Precipitated withdrawal: buprenorphine too early, naltrexone with opioids on board; QT prolongation and accumulation with methadone; hepatotoxicity with naltrexone

Insights

Affinity, not strength, precipitates withdrawal: buprenorphine binds tighter than a full agonist yet activates less, so it displaces the full agonist and receptor activity falls

The naloxone in buprenorphine-naloxone deters misuse: inactive under the tongue, it precipitates withdrawal only when the tablet is crushed and injected

Adverse effects and cautions, by drugtap to open
NaltrexoneHepatotoxicity; contraindicated with liver disease or opioid useA monthly intramuscular depot form exists
AcamprosateDiarrheaKidney-cleared: avoid with significant impairment
DisulfiramA reaction with any alcohol, alcohol-containing medicines includedNot in pregnancy or cardiac decompensation
MethadoneQT prolongation, torsades de pointes; accumulation and overdoseInhibitors of CYP3A4 (cytochrome P450 3A4) raise the level
VareniclineNausea, headaches, insomnia, abnormal dreams; depressed moodMost common: nausea and sleep disturbance
2Urgent risks
Too earlyBuprenorphine while a full agonist is still on board

If opioid withdrawal signs are not yet present, choose wait; give buprenorphine once withdrawal signs appear.

AntagonistNaltrexone requested by a patient who used opioids recently In practice:Wait at least 7 days after the last full-agonist opioid

If medically supervised withdrawal is not complete, choose not naltrexone; buprenorphine or methadone.

DrinkingDisulfiram requested by a patient still drinking

If the patient is still drinking, choose naltrexone, not disulfiram.

MethadoneSedation and slow breathing during titration or after a CYP3A4 inhibitor

If breathing slows, choose naloxone; some need an infusion and admission, as methadone is long-acting.

PregnancyOpioid use disorder in pregnancy

If she is pregnant, choose methadone or buprenorphine, not withdrawal alone.

3Differential
Which effect is it, most tempting first
EffectFingerprintDecides it
May show yawning, sweating, dilated pupils, goose flesh, hyperactive bowelTypically 4 to 48 hours after the last dose; no new drug given
Precipitated withdrawalWithdrawal right after a first buprenorphine or naltrexone doseRapid onset, more severe; a full agonist still on board
Methadone toxicitySedation, small pupils, slow breathing on methadoneDuring titration, or after a CYP3A4 inhibitor
Disulfiram reactionFlushing, throbbing headache, tachycardia, sweatingAlcohol on disulfiram, cough syrups and elixirs included
Varenicline adverse effectsNausea, insomnia, abnormal dreams, low moodStarted to quit smoking; nausea and sleep complaints lead
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Also smokes heavilyVarenicline and bupropion treat smoking, not drinkingNaltrexone or acamprosate for the alcohol
Alcohol withdrawal treated with chlordiazepoxideBenzodiazepines treat withdrawal, not the use disorderAdd a relapse drug: naltrexone or acamprosate
Smoker with anginaNot a contraindication to nicotine replacement; most data suggest it is safeNicotine replacement may be used
Pause point
Drinking daily, wants to cut down; no opioids; liver normal Offered as disulfiram, or acamprosate Still drinking: naltrexone can start now; disulfiram needs abstinence → Naltrexone
Last heroin this morning, wants maintenance today; no withdrawal signs Offered as buprenorphine now, or naltrexone No withdrawal yet: a partial agonist or an antagonist now precipitates it → Wait for withdrawal signs, then buprenorphine
7Treatment
Choose by substance and situation
SituationChooseNot
Alcohol, still drinkingNaltrexoneDisulfiram: abstinent patients only
Alcohol, abstinent; liver disease or opioid useAcamprosateNaltrexone
Alcohol, first-line drugs failed or contraindicated; 48 hours abstinent; motivated or supervisedDisulfiram In practice:An outpatient start may follow 4 or 5 days of abstinenceBenzodiazepines: they treat withdrawal only
Opioids, most patientsBuprenorphine (with naloxone) or methadone, often long term In practice:Buprenorphine can be prescribed in an office; methadone only through a licensed opioid treatment programWithdrawal management alone: high relapse
Opioids, pregnantMethadone or buprenorphineWithdrawal or abstinence alone
Opioid use disorder, mild; withdrawal completed; wants no agonistNaltrexoneNaltrexone before withdrawal is complete

Tobacco, in order of efficacy:

1

FirstMost patients; the most effective single drug

Varenicline
2

NextVarenicline not tolerated (nausea, headaches, insomnia, abnormal dreams)

Combination nicotine replacement: a patch plus gum or lozenge

The patch keeps a steady level; gum or lozenge answers a craving In practice:Combined nicotine products are about as effective as varenicline

3

ThenDepression or a weight concern

Bupropion

Not with seizure risk, bulimia or anorexia

8Follow-up
Prescribing safely
WhenCheckWhy
Methadone start and titrationECGQT prolongation; it can accumulate faster than it is cleared
Methadone with an azole, ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, fluvoxamine or cimetidineWatch for opioid toxicityCYP3A4 inhibition raises the methadone level
Acute pain on methadone or buprenorphineContinue it; add opioids for the painPain is managed as in any patient
Opioid maintenance going wellContinue; a slow taper may be tried if highly motivated, watching for relapseMany need long-term therapy
On disulfiramNo alcohol in any form, cough syrups and elixirs includedEffects may persist 3 to 7 days after the last dose
Varenicline or bupropionMood and behaviorNeuropsychiatric events were reported after marketing In practice:Trials have not confirmed a causal link, and the boxed warning was removed
Practice
  1. 44-year-old man with alcohol use disorder wants to cut down drinks 8 beers daily; strong cravings takes no opioids or other drugs AST 38 U/L · ALT 30 U/L · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Naltrexone → still drinking with cravings, no opioids and a healthy liver: naltrexone can start now; disulfiram is for abstinent patients, and chlordiazepoxide treats withdrawal, not the use disorder
  2. 51-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder and cirrhosis abstinent 3 weeks since a hospital stay cravings; afraid she will relapse; no opioids or tobacco creatinine 0.8 mg/dL · albumin 3.0 g/dL → Acamprosate → abstinent with liver disease: acamprosate is excreted mostly unchanged by the kidneys and is safe for the liver; naltrexone is contraindicated with liver disease, and disulfiram is second line
  3. 29-year-old man with opioid use disorder wants buprenorphine today last used heroin 3 hours ago calm; no yawning, sweating or goose flesh pupils 3 mm · HR 78/min · BP 124/78 mm Hg → Wait for withdrawal signs, then give buprenorphine → heroin is still on board and withdrawal has not begun: buprenorphine now would displace it and precipitate withdrawal, so the first dose waits for withdrawal signs; naltrexone needs a completed withdrawal
  4. 26-year-old woman, 11 weeks pregnant, injects heroin daily wants to stop for the baby asks to come off all opioids now HR 84/min · BP 116/72 mm Hg · urine screen positive for opiates → Buprenorphine maintenance → opioid use disorder in pregnancy: methadone or buprenorphine maintenance brings better maternal and neonatal outcomes than abstinence; withdrawal alone risks relapse, and naltrexone needs a completed withdrawal
  5. 47-year-old man on methadone maintenance for 2 years started clarithromycin 4 days ago for pneumonia now drowsy and hard to rouse; no new drug use RR 8/min · pupils 2 mm · oxygen saturation 89% → Methadone toxicity → clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and raises the methadone level: sedation, small pupils and slow breathing are opioid toxicity; withdrawal brings dilated pupils, yawning and sweating
  6. 38-year-old woman with opioid use disorder started on methadone the dose is being raised over several weeks no other medicines; no known heart disease HR 72/min · BP 118/76 mm Hg · alert, not sedated → ECG during titration → methadone prolongs the QTc and can cause torsades de pointes, so ECGs are monitored during initiation and titration; liver injury is the naltrexone concern, and kidney function the acamprosate one
  7. 52-year-old man smokes 1 pack a day and wants to quit asks for the single most effective medicine no seizures, eating disorder or psychiatric illness BP 132/84 mm Hg · HR 76/min → Varenicline → varenicline is the most effective single drug; combination nicotine replacement comes next and bupropion last; a single nicotine product is weaker than combined products
  8. 45-year-old woman taking varenicline for 3 weeks to quit smoking nausea and vivid dreams she cannot tolerate wants another medicine to stay off cigarettes BP 124/80 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Nicotine patch plus nicotine gum → varenicline side effects not tolerated: combination nicotine replacement, a patch for a steady level plus gum for cravings; combined products beat a single one, and acamprosate is an alcohol relapse drug
Pairs with Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal covers intoxication, withdrawal and overdose, naloxone included.
Other antidepressants covers bupropion and its contraindications.
Antipsychotic Adverse Effects covers clozapine levels after quitting smoking.
Transferable rule

Before any relapse drug, ask what is still on board: opioids rule out naltrexone and delay buprenorphine until withdrawal shows; alcohol rules out disulfiram; liver disease points to acamprosate, and kidney impairment rules it out.
